(i) The tidal torque is always positive, i.e., it always acts to increase the warp amplitude.
(a) the radiation-driven warps of accretion disc are stable, (b) the disc warps precess, and (c) the radiation torque is the main driving torque of the disc warps.

the dynamics, evolution, and structure of accretion flows in the context of compact binaries and X-ray binaries, and the interaction of these flows with the surrounding stellar environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a strong correlation between the presence of a warp and the X-ray source being in the hard state (or the low-hard state).
the radiation torque is the dominant torque for the warp evolution, but the tidal torque is important for the initial warp evolution.
, while the radiation-driven warps in X-ray binaries can be quite significant, they are unlikely to be large enough to affect the accretion flow significantly.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

(1) the disc warp can reach a large amplitude, which is much greater than that of the classical theory;  (2) a disc warp is a global mode, which can propagate from the inner to outer regions;  (3) a precessing disc warp can reach the outer radius of the disc; and (4) a precessed disc warp can be a stable structure.
the radiation-driven warps are very common, and they are likely the dominant warping mechanism.

(i) the tidal torque is always positive (i.e. it always opens the warp), and it is proportional to the warp amplitude and the disc aspect ratio, (ii) the radiation torque is negative for small warp amplitudes and positive for large warp amplitudes; and (iii) the disc self-shadowing is important for large warp ampltudes, and it reduces the radiation torque by about a factor of two.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the tidal torque can be neglected for all realistic parameters.
the radiation torque is always dominant over the tidal torque, except in very close systems.
the tidal and radiation torques in the outer disc are not in equilibrium.
